constraints: nums is sorted in strictly increasing order

sample_test_cases.explanation: The target value 9 exists at index 4.

hints: The array is already sorted.
Checking every element results in O(n) complexity.
Compare the target with the middle element.
Discard half of the search space after each comparison.
explanation: Binary Search works on sorted arrays by repeatedly dividing the search space into two halves. Compare the target with the middle element. If they are equal, return the index. If the target is smaller, continue searching in the left half; otherwise, search in the right half. Repeat until the target is found or the search space becomes empty. This approach runs in O(log n) time.

title: Find Peak Element
description: A peak element is an element that is strictly greater than its adjacent neighbors. Given an integer array nums, find the index of any peak element and return it. You may assume nums[-1] = nums[n] = -∞. Your solution must run in O(log n) time.
constraints: nums[i] != nums[i + 1] for all valid i

sample_test_cases.explanation: nums[2] = 3 is greater than both neighboring elements, making it a peak.

special_judge.note: For arrays containing multiple valid peak elements, any valid peak index should be accepted.

hints: A peak is greater than its immediate neighbors.
You do not need to find the highest element in the array.
Compare the middle element with its right neighbor.
If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], a peak must exist on the right side.
explanation: Use Binary Search on the array. At each step, compare nums[mid] with nums[mid + 1]. If nums[mid] is smaller, then a peak must exist somewhere on the right side because the sequence is increasing. Otherwise, a peak must exist on the left side (including mid). Repeatedly shrink the search space until a single index remains. That index will be a valid peak element. This approach runs in O(log n) time.

nums is originally sorted in ascending order and then rotated

title: Single Element in Sorted Array
description: You are given a sorted array consisting of only integers where every element appears exactly twice except for one element which appears exactly once. Return the single element that appears only once. Your solution must run in O(log n) time and O(1) space.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
All other elements appear exactly twice

sample_test_cases.explanation: All elements appear twice except 2, which appears exactly once.

hints: A linear scan works, but does not satisfy the O(log n) requirement.
Observe how pairs are positioned before and after the unique element.
Before the single element, pairs start at even indices.
After the single element, this pattern breaks.
explanation: In a perfectly paired sorted array, the first occurrence of each pair appears at an even index and the second occurrence appears at the next odd index. Once the single element appears, this pattern shifts. Use Binary Search to identify where the pattern breaks. Compare the middle element with its neighboring pair and decide which half still contains the single element. This allows finding the answer in O(log n) time and O(1) space.

title: Koko Eating Bananas
description: Koko loves to eat bananas. There are n piles of bananas, where the i-th pile contains piles[i] bananas. The guards will return in h hours. Koko can decide her eating speed k (bananas per hour). Each hour, she chooses one pile and eats up to k bananas from it. If the pile has fewer than k bananas, she eats all bananas in that pile and spends the rest of the hour doing nothing. Return the minimum integer k such that Koko can eat all the bananas within h hours.

sample_test_cases.explanation: At speed 4, Koko spends 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 hours, which is the minimum possible speed.

hints: Instead of searching for the answer directly, search for the eating speed.
If Koko can finish all bananas at speed k, she can also finish at any speed greater than k.
This monotonic property makes Binary Search applicable.
For a given speed k, calculate the total hours needed using ceiling division.
explanation: The answer lies between 1 and the largest pile size. For a candidate speed k, compute the total hours required to finish all piles using ceil(pile / k). If the total hours are less than or equal to h, then k is a valid speed and we try to find a smaller one. Otherwise, we need a larger speed. Use Binary Search on the answer space to find the minimum valid speed in O(n log M), where M is the maximum pile size.

constraints: nums1 and nums2 are sorted in non-decreasing order

sample_test_cases.explanation: The merged sorted array would be [1,2,3]. The median is 2.

hints: Merging both arrays works, but does not satisfy the required complexity.
Think about partitioning the two arrays into left and right halves.
The median is correct when every element on the left side is less than or equal to every element on the right side.
Perform Binary Search on the smaller array to find the correct partition.
explanation: Use Binary Search on the smaller array to determine a partition point. The partition divides both arrays into left and right halves such that the total number of elements on the left equals the total number on the right (or differs by one for odd lengths). The correct partition is reached when the largest element on the left side is less than or equal to the smallest element on the right side. Once found, compute the median based on whether the total number of elements is odd or even. This achieves O(log(min(m, n))) time complexity.

sample_test_cases.explanation: Split into [7,2,5] and [10,8]. The largest subarray sum is 18, which is the minimum possible.

hints: The answer is not a position in the array; it is a possible maximum subarray sum.
The minimum answer cannot be smaller than the largest element.
The maximum answer cannot exceed the sum of the entire array.
Use Binary Search on the answer space and check whether a candidate maximum sum allows splitting into at most k subarrays.
explanation: The answer lies between max(nums) and sum(nums). For a candidate value mid, greedily form subarrays while ensuring each subarray sum does not exceed mid. Count how many subarrays are needed. If more than k subarrays are required, mid is too small and must be increased. Otherwise, mid is a valid answer and we try to find a smaller one. This monotonic property allows Binary Search on the answer space, yielding an efficient O(n log(sum(nums))) solution.
